THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES · DEEP DIVE

Before 1 Million Years Ago: Every Global Hominin & Tool Site (7.0–1.0 Ma)

Every securely dated—and every seriously debated—hominin fossil and Early Stone Age / Mode 1 / Early Acheulean locality on Earth older than 1.0 million years is concentrated exclusively across Africa and parts of Eurasia and Wallacea. None exist in the Americas, Australia/New Guinea, Polynesia, or high Arctic latitudes. This guide documents every known >1 Ma locality globally, the species tied to it, and how hominins reached each frontier.

All 164 published pre-1.0 Ma fossil and archaeological localities across Africa, SW Asia, Caucasus/Anatolia, Europe, India/Pakistan, China, Java, Flores, and Sulawesi (~7.0–1.0 Ma).

African Deep Roots: Hominins, Earliest Tools & Trans-Saharan Spread (7.0–1.0 Ma)

All firmly established hominin evolutionary origins prior to ~2.5 million years ago took place inside Africa: Sahelanthropus tchadensis (~7 Ma, Chad), Orrorin tugenensis (~6 Ma, Kenya), Ardipithecus kadabba and ramidus (5.8–4.3 Ma, Ethiopia), Australopithecus (~4.3–1.98 Ma across Chad, East Africa, and South Africa), Kenyanthropus platyops (~3.5 Ma), and Paranthropus (~2.9–1.0 Ma). Stone-tool behavior emerged by ~3.3 Ma at Lomekwi 3 (unknown Pliocene maker, possibly Kenyanthropus or A. afarensis), followed by ~3.0–2.6 Ma early Oldowan flake-and-core assemblages at Nyayanga (with Paranthropus!), Namorotukunan, Ledi-Geraru Bokol Dora, East Gona, and Omo Member F. [182] [131] [129]

By ~2.44 Ma, hominin toolmakers had already crossed a humid 'Green Sahara' corridor to reach Mediterranean Algeria at Aïn Boucherit (Sahnouni et al. 2018), while by 1.76–1.3 Ma early Homo erectus carried Large Cutting Tools (Early Acheulean handaxes and cleavers) from Kokiselei 4, Olduvai FLK West, and Konso to high 2,000–2,400 m Ethiopian plateaus (Melka Kunture & Gadeb), South Africa's Rietputs 15 Vaal gravels (~1.55 Ma), and Thomas Quarry I in Morocco (~1.3 Ma). [183] [128] [146]

Out of Africa I & How Hominins Reached Eurasia & Wallacea (2.5–1.0 Ma)

Four primary physical pathways and mechanisms explain how >1 Ma hominins colonized Eurasia and Island Southeast Asia: (1) The Sinai–Jordan Rift corridor: savanna and lake chains during wet Pliocene/Early Pleistocene intervals led early Homo north through Zarqa Valley (~2.48–1.95 Ma), Erq el-Ahmar (~1.9 Ma), and later large-bodied H. erectus at ʿUbeidiya (~1.5 Ma). (2) A possible southern Red Sea (Bab el-Mandeb) or northern Green Arabia littoral pathway connecting Danakil (Buia/Engel Ela) to Nefud paleolakes and the Zarqa/Siwalik piedmont. (3) Across Anatolia, Caucasus, and Eastern European riverplains into Europe—demonstrated at Dmanisi (~1.77 Ma), Grăunceanu (~1.95 Ma cutmarks, Curran et al. 2025), Kocabaş (~1.6–1.2 Ma), Kozarnika (1.6–1.4 Ma), Korolevo I (1.42 Ma), Pirro Nord, Lézignan, Orce, Sima del Elefante ATE7-1 ('Pink', 1.4–1.1 Ma), Vallonnet (1.2 Ma), and Pont-de-Lavaud (1.1 Ma)—whereas no geological/fossil proof supports a Gibraltar Strait ocean crossing at 1.4 Ma. [147] [133] [151] [86] [77]

(4) Across the Asian steppe–loess belt and Indian piedmont into China (Shangchen 2.12 Ma, Xihoudu 2.43/1.27 Ma, Gongwangling 1.63 Ma, Yunxian 1.77 Ma, Yuanmou 1.7 Ma, Nihewan 1.66–1.1 Ma), then south across the exposed Sunda Shelf landbridge into Java (~1.5–1.3 Ma Sangiran/Mojokerto) during glacial sea-level drops. Crucially, Calio on Sulawesi (>1.04 Ma, Hakim et al. 2025 Nature) and Wolo Sege on Flores (1.02 Ma) lie beyond deep ocean straits (Wallace's Line) that never dried out; small founding hominin groups likely crossed these straits via accidental storm-surge or tsunami vegetation rafting. [63] [66] [92] [184]

Transparent boundaries on contested claims & empty continents: Several claimed pre-2 Ma Eurasian/Crete traces—including Crete Trachilos prints (~5.7 Ma), NW India Masol (~2.6 Ma), Germany Untermaßfeld (~1.05 Ma), Taman Kermek/Dagestan Muhkai, and China Renzidong/Longgupo mandible affinities—are plotted explicitly with clear cautions because geofact fracture kinematics, stratigraphic reworking, or non-hominin anatomy remain unresolved. Conversely, Zero confirmed >1 Ma hominin sites exist in the Americas, Sahul/Australia, Pacific islands, Greenland, or high Arctic tundra, which were not reached until Homo sapiens (or Denisovan/Siberian ancestors in northeast Eurasia) much later. [127] [164] [160] [167]

(Tectonic tilting of the Rift beds leaves precise bed-by-bed radiometric constraints challenging)[57] [58]
KonsoAbout 1.4 million years agoHominins UnassignedA worked bone preserves deliberate flake removals and evidence interpreted as use, extending the known range of early tool materials. (The specimen was recovered from the surface rather than excavated in an intact occupation floor)[11]
Morgaon & Bori (Deccan Basalt, Maharashtra, India) [Age Debated]~1.4–0.8 million years ago (tephra age debated)Homo Erectus, Hominins UnassignedIn situ basalt-flake Acheulean cleavers and handaxes buried below reverse-polarity alluvial clays on the Karha and Kukdi rivers alongside Attirampakkam (1.5 Ma) and Isampur (1.2 Ma). How they… (YTT-like (74 ka) vs Early Pleistocene reworked tephra dates remain actively debated at Bori)[59]

How they got there: Northeastward… (No skeletal hominin remains recovered in Nihewan fluvio-lacustrine silts)[171] [172]
Ash-Shuwayhitiyah (Al-Jawf, N. Saudi Arabia) [Age Debated]~1.3–1.0 Ma (provisional; radiometric age debated)Homo Erectus, Hominins UnassignedQuartzite choppers, polyhedrons, and spheroids discovered along northern Arabian drainage channels (Whalen 1986; Petraglia 2003), frequently invoked for the 'Green Arabia' corridor linking… (Surface lag context lacks direct burial OSL/cosmogenic chronology, leaving its true pre-1 Ma vs Middle Pleistocene age unresolved)[181]
Banshan (1.32 Ma) & Feiliang (1.2 Ma), Nihewan Basin (Hebei, China)1.32–1.20 million years agoHomo ErectusSuccessive fine-grained lakeshore horizons with high artifact-refitting sets proving systematic local chert procurement and short-term carcass processing across seasonal paleolake… (Lithic-only assemblages; seasonality constraints remain modeled from pollen/faunal teeth)[173] [172]
Fuente Nueva-3 (Orce, Guadix-Baza Basin, Spain)~1.3–1.2 million years agoEarly Homo, Homo AntecessorLimestone hammerstones and flint Mode 1 flakes clustered directly around a Mammuthus meridionalis carcass scavenged competitively with giant hyenas (Pachycrocuta brevirostris), complementing… (Radiometric/ESR age uncertainties place Orce between ~1)[73] [74]
Thomas Quarry IAt least ~1.3 Ma; Unit L chronostratigraphyHominins UnassignedAcheulean toolmaking is documented in an older, stratified part of the Casablanca quarry. (This occupation context is distinct from the younger cave fossils)[29]
Gona BSN12Approximately 1.262 ± 0.034 million years agoHomo ErectusA partial cranium and both Oldowan and Acheulean tools are associated with the Boolihinan Tuff. (Tuff adhering to fossils and tools strengthens their association; unrelated surface artifacts are less secure)[24]
Gediz River / Kula (Manisa, Western Anatolia, Turkey)1.24–1.17 million years agoHomo Erectus, Hominins UnassignedIn situ struck quartzite flake discovered stratified directly beneath precisely 40Ar/39Ar-dated basalt lava terraces along the Gediz River (Maddy et al. 2015), providing an unimpeachably… (Single diagnostic artifact recovered directly within the basalt-bracketed river gravel)[153]
Grotte du Vallonnet (Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, SE France)1.2–1.1 million years agoEarly Homo, Homo AntecessorCoastal Ligurian limestone cave sealed beneath U-Pb-dated stalagmites (~1.22–1.13 Ma, Michel et al. 2017) containing limestone/quartzite choppers, flakes, and cut-marked deer/bovid bones. How… (Modest artifact assemblage (~100 pieces); debate over minor marine beach-cobble component)[158]
Isampur Quarry (Hunsgi–Baichbal Basin, Karnataka)c. 1.27 Ma–700,000 years agoHomo ErectusReveals an intact Early Pleistocene quarry workshop beside a palaeostream where hominins wedged limestone slabs into large Acheulean cleavers, handaxes and hammers. (ESR age estimates on tooth enamel carry wider uncertainties than volcanic-tephra sites)[62] [61]
Olorgesailie Member 1–7 (Southern Kenya Rift)1.20–0.99 million years agoHomo Erectus, Hominins UnassignedDense carpets of hundreds of volcanic-lava Acheulean handaxes (Member 1 dated ~992 ka) paired with Theropithecus oswaldi baboon and hippo butchery. How they got there: Thriving seasonal Rift… (Later KNM-OG 45500 hominin frontal (~900 ka) postdates Member 1 slightly)[143]
Simbiro IIIMore than 1.2 million years agoHominins UnassignedAn unusually concentrated assemblage records skilled use of volcanic glass for bifacial tools in the Ethiopian highlands. (The point is a minimum-age marker, not an exact occupation date)[18]
Cenjiawan & Donggutuo (Nihewan Basin, Hebei, China)~1.1 million years agoHomo Erectus3D technological refitting at Cenjiawan (~1.1 Ma, Ma et al. 2024 PNAS) uncovered predetermined core-preparation strategies ~300 kyr before Europe/Africa, demonstrating unexpected East Asian… (Lithic refits without associated human skulls; Donggutuo wedges (~1)[174] [172]

How they got there: High-elevation… (Lacks associated hominin skeletal fossils; toolmaker attributed to African H)[177]
Pont-de-Lavaud & Lunery (Loire Valley / Berry, Central France)~1.1–1.05 million years agoEarly Homo, Homo AntecessorNorthwesternmost confirmed pre-1 Ma sites in Europe (~47°N), yielding >8,000 bipolar quartz Mode 1 pieces on high Creuse and Cher river terraces (Despriée et al. 2006, 2018). How they got… (No hominin skeletal remains preserved in acidic Loire quartz gravels)[159] [79]
Untermaßfeld (Thuringia, Germany) [Disputed]~1.05 million years ago (anthropic claim strongly disputed)Hominins UnassignedExceptionally rich Werra River floodplain bonebed (~1.05 Ma) where García et al. argued for rare stone tools and hominin cutmarks. If verified, it would mark >50°N Early Pleistocene hominin… (Excavation director R)[160]
Wolo Sege (So'a Basin, Flores, Indonesia)c. 1.02 million years agoHominins Unassigned, Homo ErectusProves hominins crossed deep tectonic straits east of Wallace's Line to settle Flores by one million years ago—ancestral to later small-bodied Mata Menge (~700 ka) and Homo floresiensis (~60 ka). (Basaltic stone artifacts without associated skeletal fossils in 1)[91] [92]
Dursunlu (Konya Basin, Central Anatolia, Turkey)~1.0–0.9 million years agoHomo Erectus, Hominins UnassignedQuartz core-and-flake assemblage and butchered wetland mammals recovered deep within Central Anatolian lignite seams (Güleç et al. 1999). How they got there: Across Central Anatolian lake… (Chronology rests on biochronological vole/mammal correlation and Matuyama polarity prior to Jaramillo-Brunhes shifts)[154] [152]
Engel Ela & Mulhuli-Amo (Danakil Depression, Eritrea)~1.0 million years agoHomo ErectusUA 31 cranium/pelvis (Buia) and nearby Mulhuli-Amo parietal/occipital bones with Acheulean handaxes directly overlooking the Red Sea coastal margin of Eritrea. How they got there: Northern… (Morphology blends classic African H)[144]
Trinil (Solo River, East Java, Indonesia)~1.0 Ma–500 ka (shell engraving 540–430 ka)Homo ErectusEugène Dubois's 1891 discovery of the holotype Homo erectus skullcap (Trinil 2) and femur, plus Joordens et al.'s (2015) zigzag-engraved freshwater Pseudodon mussel shell. How they got there:… (Old 1890s Main Bonebed excavation spans ~1)[175] [69]
Vallparadís (Terrassa, Catalonia, Spain)~1.0–0.83 million years agoEarly Homo, Homo AntecessorDeep lakeside Mode 1 quartz/flint flake sequence alongside butchered hippopotamus and rhinoceros remains in NE Iberia immediately before the Matuyama–Brunhes reversal. How they got there:… (Combined ESR/magnetostratigraphic revisions bracket peak Layer EVT7 close to ~0)[178] [79]
Ca' Belvedere di Monte Poggiolo (Emilia-Romagna, Italy)~1.0–0.85 million years agoEarly Homo, Homo AntecessorOver 4,000 exceptionally sharp refitting flint flakes and unidirectional cores deposited in paleo-coastal gravels during northern Adriatic Po Plain lowstands. How they got there: Early… (Debate persists over whether age sits right before the ~0)[161] [79]
Evron Quarry (Western Galilee Coastal Plain, Israel)~1.0–0.8 million years agoHomo ErectusMediterranean coastal-plain Acheulean bifaces, small flakes, and fauna preserving AI-detected invisible heat-exposure signatures (~500 °C) on flint and bone (Stepka et al. 2022). How they got… (Absence of visible hearth ash lenses means heat signatures could involve earliest opportunistic or incipient fire control)[179]
Calio & Talepu (Walanae Basin, South Sulawesi)c. 1.0 Ma–118 thousand years agoHominins UnassignedDeep-time Wallacean island archaeology proving repeated Early & Middle Pleistocene oceanic crossings to Sulawesi by unknown archaic hominins hundreds of millennia before modern Homo sapiens. (No hominin body fossils recovered from pre-sapiens Walanae beds)[92] [93]
Barranc de la Boella (Tarragona, Spain)~1.0–0.8 million years ago (Unit II ~0.99 Ma)Early Homo, Homo AntecessorLarge Acheulean schist picks and crude cleavers alongside a butchered Mammuthus meridionalis skeleton on an ancient Francolí delta (Vallverdú et al. 2014; Ollé et al. 2023)—Europe's oldest… (Span across the Matuyama-Jaramillo transition permits dates between ~1)[162] [163]
Buia Uadi AaladAbout 1 million years agoHominins UnassignedA cranium from Eritrea preserves a mosaic of features relevant to variation within early Homo. (The original report describes mixed erectus-like and sapiens-like traits)[16]
DakaAbout 1 million years agoHomo ErectusA cranial vault and associated fossil discoveries extend the African Homo erectus record into the early Middle Pleistocene transition. (Morphological similarity does not establish a mapped migration route or identify a direct ancestor of a living population)[15]
TighennifProbably ≥1.0 Ma; revised biochronology, uncertainHominins UnassignedMandibles and other hominin remains occur with an Acheulean assemblage; their precise taxonomic placement remains debated. (The older ~700 ka estimate and later ≥1 Ma interpretation differ)[27] [28]
Wonderwerk — Acheulean fire tracesAbout 1 million years agoHominins UnassignedBurned bone and plant ash within Acheulean sediments provide evidence of fire inside the cave. (Microscopic burning evidence is distinct from proof of making fire or a permanently occupied home)[35] [33]
